edges.effect_quant: In a 10-year community cohort of 873 older adults, the highest visceral-fat area tertile in men showed significantly faster MMSE decline than the lowest tertile. In 9,189 adults from population-based cohorts, higher visceral adipose tissue quartiles were associated with lower cognitive scores and more vascular brain injury. In 674 dementia-free 70-year-olds, higher visceral fat accumulation was associated with thinner cortex, a brain-health pattern compatible with later cognitive vulnerability.
edges.population: middle-aged and older adults with abdominal fat quantification by imaging and cognitive assessment
edges.mechanism: High visceral fat promotes inflammatory signaling, insulin resistance, vascular dysfunction, and adverse adipokine profiles. Those pathways can affect white matter, perfusion, and cortical integrity, which makes later cognitive decline more plausible than in people with less visceral adiposity.
edges.summary: The clearest conclusion is that high visceral fat is a harmful brain-aging signal, especially in older adults. Longitudinal and cross-sectional data both suggest that people carrying more visceral adiposity show worse cognitive trajectories or worse structural brain correlates than leaner peers.
edges.caveats: Not every study finds the same sex-specific pattern, and some of the evidence relies on intermediate brain markers rather than incident dementia. This edge is strongest for cognitive aging risk, not for a deterministic prediction that high visceral fat will inevitably cause dementia.

evidence.citation: Kazuaki Uchida et al 2024 J Nutr Health Aging
evidence.notes: Association between abdominal adiposity and cognitive decline in older adults: a 10-year community-based study.
